1.​ Definition and general requirements
          1.1 Definition
             ●​ Tabards is a generic term used to describe the cloth worn upon the armor. It is made to
                show the heraldry of the wearer and prove your wealth and status on the battlefield, or
                in the list.
             ●​ Nowadays, tabards have the same function as a sports jersey: to indicate the team you
                belong to.

          1.2 Types of tabards
             ●​ Sleeveless tabard : Tabards without sleeves. Simple design, common in the 13th
                century and 14th century. Tend to be rare in the 15th century.
             ●​ Short-sleeves tabard : Tabards with short sleeves that can go up to the elbow.
                Common design in the 14th century. Tend to be rare in the 15th century.
             ●​ Long-sleeves tabard : Tabards with long sleeves that cover the whole arms, from
                shoulder to hand. Common design in the 14th and the 15th century.
             ●​ Eastern tabard : We do not have many historical references for eastern tabard. It is
                allowed to use the same tabard as European armors. Eastern stylization of tabard are
                displayed in the document “Eastern Armors”.
             ●​ Exception for full plates armors : Wearing full plates armor makes the use of tabard not
                practical. Therefore, it is allowed to wear only a scarf. Scarf must follow the general
                requirements (1.3).

1.3 Material requirements
          All tabards and scarf must must respect the following requirements:
             ●​ Shapes, decorations and designs must be based on historical sources.
             ●​ Tabards must conform to the Textiles and Leather rules document.
             ●​ Tabards can be made of the following materials:
                     ○​ Wool
                     ○​ Linen
                     ○​ Silk
                     ○​ Coton
                     ○​ Any other material based on historical sources.
             ●​ Tabards can be made of modern materials in the following cases:
                     ○​ The modern material replicates the aesthetic of an approved material listed in
                        1.3.2
                     ○​ The modern material is strong enough to endure full contact fights and to not be
                        damaged too easily.
                     ○​ We recommend asking for approval of the Authenticity Committee regarding
                        tabard made of modern materials before placing an order.

          1.4 Fastening systems requirements
             ●​ Tabards can be tied with the following systems:
                     ○​ Buttons made of fabric, wood, bone, or metal.
                     ○​ Laces, made of leather, rope or fabric.
                     ○​ Any other system based on historical sources.
                     ○​ Any modern fastening system is denied. (Zips, snap buttons, velcro, paracord,
                        nylon rope etc.)
             ●​ Tabards can be open on the side, tied with laces.
             ●​ Tabards can be open on the front, and tied with buttons.

          1.5 Colors requirements
             ●​ Colors used for tabards must be based on historical sources. Any clearly modern color
                is denied. (Neon pink, fluorescent yellow etc.)
             ●​ For the Marshal's safety, the use of yellow as a main color of a tabard is denied. Yellow
                color must represent less than 50% of the tabard colors. The combination of black and
                yellow must not be inspired by Marshal’s uniforms.

          1.6 Symbols and decorations requirements
             ●​ Symbols and decorations used for tabards must be based on historical sources. Any
                clearly modern symbol or decoration is denied. (Warhammer logo, movies or TV show
                imagery, modern slogan etc.)
             ●​ We recommend taking inspiration from middle ages manuscripts to create your
                symbols.




Tabards                                                                                 3

●​ Symbols and decorations used for tabards must be made with the following
                techniques:
                    ○​ Embroidery.
                    ○​ Painting: can be by hand or by stamp.
                    ○​ Sewing a patchwork of clothes to create a design.
                    ○​ Any other techniques based on historical sources.

          1.7 Exception for cuirass
             ●​ When wearing a cuirass, it is allowed to wear the tabard under it. In this case, it is also
                allowed to wear the pauldrons upon the tabard.

2.​ Sleeveless tabard
          2.1 Historical sources and datation
             ●​ Sleeveless tabard is an easy way to display your heraldic. This type of tabard has been
                used all along the middle-ages, from knight templars to late 15th century armors.
             ●​ They are approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.




                       A​                               B​                             C


          A: Life of Eustace and Other Saints - 1300 - France ​
          B: Weltchronik - 1360 - Germany
          C: Bibliothèque de Besançon - 1410 - France

          2.2 Specific requirements
             ●​ Sleeveless tabard must follow the general requirements
             ●​ Sleeveless tabard must not be too long.
             ●​ Knee is the limit, tabard must not go below.

3.​ Short-sleeves tabard
          3.1 Historical sources and datation
             ●​ Short-sleeves tabard is the main design of the 14th century and later. Its simple shape
                makes it easy to craft and to wear. Many different designs can be documented by
                historical sources
             ●​ They are approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.




                      A​                                B​                           C

          A: Bible historiale - 1360 - France
          B: Weltchronik - 1360 - Germany
          C: Office of the Feast of Corpus Christi - 1403 - Austria




Tabards                                                                                7

3.2 Specific requirements
             ●​ Short-sleeves tabard must follow the general requirements
             ●​ Short-sleeves tabard must not be too long. Knee is the limit.
             ●​ The sleeves must not be too long. Elbow is the limit, unless it can be documented by
                historical sources.
             ●​ The sleeves can be open or plain (as a shirt).

4.​ Long-Sleeves tabard
          4.1 Historical sources and datation
             ●​ Long-sleeves tabard combine the role of exposing your heraldry and protecting your
                armor. The sleeves often cover the whole arm, up to the wrist, but can be shorter (up to
                mid-forearm). Many different designs can be documented by historical sources.
             ●​ They are approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.




           A​                          B​                          C​                             D

          A: Guiron le Courtois - 1380 - France
          B: Knebel von Katzenelnbogen - 1401 - Germany
          C: Bible historiale, BL Royal 15 D III - 1420 - France
          D: Le Livre et le vraye hystoire du bon roy Alixandre - 1420 - France

          4.2 Specific requirements
             ●​ Long-sleeves tabard must follow the general requirements
             ●​ Long-sleeves tabard must not be too long. Knee is the limit.
             ●​ The sleeves must cover the arm up to the middle of the forearm as a minimum.
             ●​ The sleeves must be plain (as a shirt).
